To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Malaysian economy has undergone rapid industrialization and urbanization since independence in 1957, and that this has been accompanied by a significant increase in the size and strength of the organized trade unions.
the industrial relations system of Malaysia has undergone significant changes since 1950, with the government playing a more active role, but the system still remains voluntarist in nature.

the Malaysian government has been increasingly active in the industrial relations field, and this has had the effect of reducing the scope of voluntarism and collective bargaining, and of increasing the role of government in industrial relations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions. (1) What is the position of labour within the Malaysian economy?

the following questions: What is the position of labour within the Malaysian economy? What has been the evolution of the industrial relations systems and what is their current position? How have government policies influenced this development?

the following questions: What is the position of labour within the Malaysian economy? How does this relate to the economic development strategy pursued by the Government of Malaysia? What is the nature of the Malaysian industrial relations system and what is the position of the labour movement within this system? How does this compare with the industrial relations systems of the other countries of South East Asia?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the industrial relations system has become increasingly rigid and inflexible, and the position of workers in the economy has been weakened.

the Malaysian government has not been able to reconcile its commitment to the development strategy of import substitution and light manufacturing export with the maintenance of the traditional voluntaristic system of industrial relations.
the position of labour has been weakened in the industrial relations system and the prospects for the future do not appear to be bright.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the industrial relations system has been transformed into one in which the government has become increasingly interventionist in the interests of development, but in the process has eroded the voluntarist tradition which had previously characterised industrial relations in Malaysia.

Malaysia has been able to achieve a high rate of economic growth by a strategy that has relied heavily on foreign investment and the export of labour-intensive manufactured goods, with the result that the country has been able to avoid the worst effects of the international recession.
the government has sought to create a system of industrial relations that is conducive to the needs of capital and to its own political interests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the government has been able to use the Industrial Relations Act as an instrument to control the labour movement.
Malaysia is not a good place to work, and the Malaysian government does not care about workers’ rights.
the industrial relations system has become more formalized and less responsive to the needs of workers.
